========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. Um, so, what brings me in... well, it's a lot of things, I guess, but mostly it's just been getting to this point where I feel like I absolutely cannot settle in my own body anymore. It’s the strangest feeling, almost like there’s a motor running inside me that I can’t switch off. 

And it really flares up, like, especially when I’m supposed to just sit quietly and do the things I need to do—like handling the household paperwork or sitting down to go over shared household plans. My husband will want to sit at the dining table on a Sunday morning and just figure out the week, look at the bills, you know, normal adult stuff, and I just... I can't sit there. I'm shifting in my chair, I'm getting up to grab a glass of water, I'm tapping my foot, and it feels physically uncomfortable to just be still and focus on the paper in front of me. 

I mean, I have a bachelor's degree, I used to be able to push through this kind of stuff when I was younger, but lately, being at home and trying to manage the day-to-day admin of our lives... it's like my body is just rebelling against sitting quietly. I just feel so restless all the time, like I have to be up and doing something, anything, other than sitting there looking at those plans. And it's exhausting, honestly, because I want to just be able to sit and get it done, but I just can't seem to make my body cooperate.

Anxious or worried... um, no, not really. I mean, it's not a feeling of fear or worry, you know? And if I manage to stop doing that with my hands, then my foot starts bouncing. Just this rapid, continuous tapping on the floor. My husband will sometimes just gently put his hand on my knee to get me to stop, and I don't even realize I'm doing it until he does that. 

And it's the same thing at family dinners, too. You know, when you go over to someone's house and everyone is sitting around the dining table for an hour or two just talking? I try so hard to look composed and just be present in the conversation, but I'm constantly shifting my weight, crossing and uncrossing my legs, adjusting how I'm sitting. I feel like I must look so uncomfortable to everyone else, but really, it's just that staying in one position for more than a few minutes feels almost impossible. I'll lean forward on my elbows, then I'll lean back, then I'll turn sideways in the chair... it's just this constant, low-level need to be in motion, even when I'm really trying my hardest to just sit still and be a normal person having dinner. It's just... always there, this physical need to fidget or move some part of my body.

I don't have racing thoughts about bad things happening or anything like that. I just have this overwhelming urge to escape the chair and the stillness. It’s like my energy has nowhere to go, and it just builds up until I have to stand up and walk into the kitchen, even if I don't actually need anything in the kitchen. I just need to break the stillness. So, yeah, not anxious, just... incredibly restless and frustrated by it.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel this strong urge to move and inability to sit still in other situations besides doing household paperwork or planning?\n\nPatient: Yes, oh, absolutely. Oh, wow, yes. Looking back... I mean, when I really think about it, this was already a huge part of who I was all the way back in elementary school. I can picture it so clearly now. I was absolutely that girl in class. You know, the one with the completely disastrous, messy desk? Like, if you lifted the top of my desk, it was just an avalanche of crumpled up assignments, half-eaten erasers, and, oh my gosh, the forgotten permission slips. My mom used to get so incredibly frustrated with me because I’d pull out a permission slip for a field trip or a pizza party that was supposed to be signed three weeks ago, and it would just be buried at the very bottom of my backpack, completely destroyed and stained with juice. 

But as for the sitting still part... yeah, definitely. My parents actually kept all my old report cards in this big box in their attic, and there were always notes from the teachers in the margins. Always. It was never about me being a bad kid or anything, but they would always write things like, "She talks out of turn," or "She seems unable to stay seated during lesson time." I remember my third-grade teacher—I think her name was Mrs. Davis—she actually had to move my desk right up next to hers because I was constantly up, wandering over to the pencil sharpener even if my pencil was fine, or leaning all the way out of my chair to talk to the kid next to me. 

I just couldn't stay glued to the chair. It felt like absolute torture to just sit there with my hands folded while she talked about fractions or geography or whatever. My legs would get that same restless feeling I was just telling you about with the paperwork. So, yes, the fidgeting and the not being able to stay put, and the talking when I wasn't supposed to... that is definitely not a new thing for me at all. It's like I’ve been doing this exact same dance my entire life, honestly, just in different chairs.

Well, yes, honestly, it really has. I mean, since I'm not currently working a traditional job right now—I've been staying home and focusing on managing the household and volunteering—you might think it wouldn't be as big of an issue, but it absolutely is. It's just a different kind of fallout.

I'll sign up to coordinate the silent auction items, which involves reaching out to local businesses, keeping track of donations in this massive spreadsheet, and making sure everything gets picked up on time. And in my head, I have this beautiful vision of how perfectly organized it's going to be. But then... the reality sets in. I'll sit down to make the phone calls, and I'll get distracted by an email, and then three hours later I'm deep-cleaning the pantry and I haven't made a single call. 

And then the deadlines start looming, and I'm scrambling, and inevitably, things slip through the cracks. I'll forget to follow up with a major donor, or I'll lose the physical donation form they handed me at a meeting because I just shoved it into my purse instead of filing it. And it's so incredibly embarrassing, because the other women on the committee—they're all so put-together and on top of things, and I feel like the chaotic one who is always dropping the ball. The fallout has been that people at home and in my volunteer circles just... they can’t reliably count on me. They know I have a good heart, but they also know I'm a wild card. 

In fact, recently, I actually had to step back from being the co-chair of the spring carnival. I had to tell them I couldn't do it this year, which broke my heart because I love the creative part of it, coming up with the game ideas and the themes. But I just couldn't handle the logistics, and I was so terrified of letting everyone down again. I keep letting things fall through despite trying so, so hard to keep all the plates spinning. 

And it affects things at home with my husband, too. He's incredibly patient, but I know it wears on him. Like, he'll ask me to call the plumber about the leaky faucet in the guest bathroom, and I'll say, "Yes, absolutely, I'll do it today." And then a week goes by, and the faucet is still leaking, and he has to ask me again. And it's not that I don't care, or that I'm trying to be difficult, it's just that my brain literally cannot hold onto that task and execute it when it needs to happen. It creates this underlying tension, you know? Because he feels like he has to manage me, or double-check that I've actually done the things I said I would do. And I hate that. I hate feeling like a child who needs to be supervised in my own marriage. So, yeah, it definitely interferes. It really, really does.

I'll sit down to make the phone calls, and I'll get distracted by an email, and then three hours later I'm deep-cleaning the pantry and I haven't made a single call. \n\nAnd then the deadlines start looming, and I'm scrambling, and inevitably, things slip through the cracks. I'll forget to follow up with a major donor, or I'll lose the physical donation form they handed me at a meeting because I just shoved it into my purse instead of filing it. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Oh, my goodness, yes. It's actually ridiculous how easily distracted I get. It's almost comical if it wasn't so frustrating. Like, just the other day—and this happens all the time, honestly, it's a daily struggle—but if I’m trying to work at the kitchen table, which is sort of my central command station for all the household bills and those PTA spreadsheets I mentioned earlier... I'll sit down with my laptop, I'll have my coffee, and I'm fully intending to just power through and get it done. 

But then, the tiniest thing happens. My phone will buzz. Just a tiny little vibration against the wood of the table—maybe it's a group text or just an alert about a sale at a craft store—and boom, my attention is just gone. I have to look at it. Or it doesn't even have to be inside the house! A car will drive by outside, maybe it's the delivery truck or just a neighbor driving a little too fast, and I'll look up out the window to see who it is. Next thing I know, I'm staring out at the street, wondering if the mail has come yet or noticing that the bushes need trimming. 

And sometimes it's not even an external noise, you know? It's my own brain! I'll be right in the middle of typing a sentence, and a totally random thought about dinner will pop into my head. I'll suddenly think, "Oh, wait, did I take the chicken out of the freezer to thaw?" or "Do we have enough of that specific pasta my youngest likes?" And that one thought can pull me completely off track. I'll get up, walk to the kitchen, start digging through the freezer, maybe reorganize a shelf while I'm in there... and it all happens before I even notice I’ve completely stopped what I was doing. Half an hour will go by, my laptop screen will have gone black, and I'm standing in the kitchen holding a bag of frozen peas, totally derailed from my actual task because every little noise or random thought just completely hijacks my attention.

My husband will want to sit at the dining table on a Sunday morning and just figure out the week, look at the bills, you know, normal adult stuff, and I just... I can't sit there. I'm shifting in my chair, I'm getting up to grab a glass of water, I'm tapping my foot, and it feels physically uncomfortable to just be still and focus on the paper in front of me. \n\nI mean, I have a bachelor's degree, I used to be able to push through this kind of stuff when I was younger, but lately, being at home and trying to manage the day-to-day admin of our lives... it's like my body is just rebelling against sitting quietly. I just feel so restless all the time, like I have to be up and doing something, anything, other than sitting there looking at those plans. And it's exhausting, honestly, because I want to just be able to sit and get it done, but I just can't seem to make my body cooperate.\n\nDoctor: Do you often act on impulse without thinking things through?\n\nPatient: Act on impulse... hmm. No, honestly, I don't think I do. It’s actually kind of the opposite, in a way? \n\nLike, I know I just said my body is always going, and I'm always jumping up from the table, but that’s not really me making a rash decision, you know? That’s just me physically needing to move. But as far as actually doing things without thinking them through—like, making big decisions out of nowhere or just jumping into things blindly—I really don't see myself doing that. \n\nI mean, I spend so much time at home now, and I have all this time to think. Probably too much time to think, honestly. Like just the other day, I was looking out at the front garden and thinking about moving the hydrangeas because they aren't getting enough morning sun, and I didn't just go grab a shovel and start digging them up on a whim. I paced around the yard, sure, but I thought about the soil, and the shade, and I looked it up on my phone for like twenty minutes while walking in circles on the grass. \n\nSo, no, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive. My husband might say I'm scattered, sure, because I'm always up and down and all over the house, but I don't just leap before I look. I definitely think things through. Sometimes I think about them so much that I don't even end up doing the thing at all, but yeah, acting without thinking isn't really something I've noticed myself doing.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious or worried when you're trying to sit and focus on tasks like household paperwork?\n\nPatient: Anxious or worried... um, no, not really. I mean, it's not a feeling of fear or worry, you know? It's not like I'm sitting there looking at the electric bill and thinking, \"Oh my gosh, what if we can't pay this?\" or \"What if I do the math wrong and everything falls apart?\" It's not that kind of dread. \n\nIt's more... it's just this intense, physical frustration. Like, my brain is saying, \"Okay, we are going to sit here and we are going to sort these papers into the 'keep' pile and the 'shred' pile,\" and my body is just screaming, \"No! We need to get up! We need to go check if the laundry is done! We need to see if the mail came!\" \n\nSo it's not anxiety, exactly. I don't feel nervous. I just feel... trapped, I guess? Like I'm being forced to wear a sweater that's too tight and itchy, and I just want to rip it off. And then I start getting annoyed with myself because I know I should just be able to sit there and do it. My husband is just sitting there calmly, drinking his coffee, highlighting things, and I'm practically vibrating out of my chair. \n\nBut no, I wouldn't call it worry. I don't have racing thoughts about bad things happening or anything like that. I just have this overwhelming urge to escape the chair and the stillness. It’s like my energy has nowhere to go, and it just builds up until I have to stand up and walk into the kitchen, even if I don't actually need anything in the kitchen. I just need to break the stillness. So, yeah, not anxious, just... incredibly restless and frustrated by it.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel this strong urge to move and inability to sit still in other situations besides doing household paperwork or planning?\n\nPatient: Yes, oh, absolutely. It's definitely not just the paperwork or the Sunday planning sessions with my husband. It really bleeds into pretty much everything where I'm expected to just... stay put. \n\nLike, for instance, when we go to church. I really do want to be there, and I want to be respectful and listen to the sermon, but I swear, the minute I sit down in that pew, it starts. I'm constantly twisting my wedding ring around and around on my finger, or I'm taking it off and putting it back on, over and over. And if I manage to stop doing that with my hands, then my foot starts bouncing. Just this rapid, continuous tapping on the floor. My husband will sometimes just gently put his hand on my knee to get me to stop, and I don't even realize I'm doing it until he does that. \n\nAnd it's the same thing at family dinners, too. You know, when you go over to someone's house and everyone is sitting around the dining table for an hour or two just talking? I try so hard to look composed and just be present in the conversation, but I'm constantly shifting my weight, crossing and uncrossing my legs, adjusting how I'm sitting. I feel like I must look so uncomfortable to everyone else, but really, it's just that staying in one position for more than a few minutes feels almost impossible. I'll lean forward on my elbows, then I'll lean back, then I'll turn sideways in the chair... it's just this constant, low-level need to be in motion, even when I'm really trying my hardest to just sit still and be a normal person having dinner. It's just... always there, this physical need to fidget or move some part of my body.\n\nDoctor: Did you experience difficulties with sitting still or fidgeting when you were a child?\n\nPatient: Oh, wow, yes. Looking back... I mean, when I really think about it, this was already a huge part of who I was all the way back in elementary school. I can picture it so clearly now. I was absolutely that girl in class. You know, the one with the completely disastrous, messy desk? Like, if you lifted the top of my desk, it was just an avalanche of crumpled up assignments, half-eaten erasers, and, oh my gosh, the forgotten permission slips. My mom used to get so incredibly frustrated with me because I’d pull out a permission slip for a field trip or a pizza party that was supposed to be signed three weeks ago, and it would just be buried at the very bottom of my backpack, completely destroyed and stained with juice. \n\nBut as for the sitting still part... yeah, definitely. My parents actually kept all my old report cards in this big box in their attic, and there were always notes from the teachers in the margins. Always. It was never about me being a bad kid or anything, but they would always write things like, \"She talks out of turn,\" or \"She seems unable to stay seated during lesson time.\" I remember my third-grade teacher—I think her name was Mrs. Davis—she actually had to move my desk right up next to hers because I was constantly up, wandering over to the pencil sharpener even if my pencil was fine, or leaning all the way out of my chair to talk to the kid next to me. \n\nI just couldn't stay glued to the chair. It felt like absolute torture to just sit there with my hands folded while she talked about fractions or geography or whatever. My legs would get that same restless feeling I was just telling you about with the paperwork. So, yes, the fidgeting and the not being able to stay put, and the talking when I wasn't supposed to... that is definitely not a new thing for me at all. It's like I’ve been doing this exact same dance my entire life, honestly, just in different chairs.\n\nDoctor: Have your symptoms interfered with your ability to work or maintain relationships?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, honestly, it really has. I mean, since I'm not currently working a traditional job right now—I've been staying home and focusing on managing the household and volunteering—you might think it wouldn't be as big of an issue, but it absolutely is. It's just a different kind of fallout. \n\nLike, with my volunteer work... I'm heavily involved with the PTA at my kids' school, and I also help organize the annual charity auction for our church. And I have the best intentions, I really do. I'll sign up to coordinate the silent auction items, which involves reaching out to local businesses, keeping track of donations in this massive spreadsheet, and making sure everything gets picked up on time. And in my head, I have this beautiful vision of how perfectly organized it's going to be. But then... the reality sets in. I'll sit down to make the phone calls, and I'll get distracted by an email, and then three hours later I'm deep-cleaning the pantry and I haven't made a single call. \n\nAnd then the deadlines start looming, and I'm scrambling, and inevitably, things slip through the cracks. I'll forget to follow up with a major donor, or I'll lose the physical donation form they handed me at a meeting because I just shoved it into my purse instead of filing it. And it's so incredibly embarrassing, because the other women on the committee—they're all so put-together and on top of things, and I feel like the chaotic one who is always dropping the ball. The fallout has been that people at home and in my volunteer circles just... they can’t reliably count on me. They know I have a good heart, but they also know I'm a wild card. \n\nIn fact, recently, I actually had to step back from being the co-chair of the spring carnival. I had to tell them I couldn't do it this year, which broke my heart because I love the creative part of it, coming up with the game ideas and the themes. But I just couldn't handle the logistics, and I was so terrified of letting everyone down again. I keep letting things fall through despite trying so, so hard to keep all the plates spinning. \n\nAnd it affects things at home with my husband, too. He's incredibly patient, but I know it wears on him. Like, he'll ask me to call the plumber about the leaky faucet in the guest bathroom, and I'll say, \"Yes, absolutely, I'll do it today.\" And then a week goes by, and the faucet is still leaking, and he has to ask me again. And it's not that I don't care, or that I'm trying to be difficult, it's just that my brain literally cannot hold onto that task and execute it when it needs to happen. It creates this underlying tension, you know? Because he feels like he has to manage me, or double-check that I've actually done the things I said I would do. And I hate that. I hate feeling like a child who needs to be supervised in my own marriage. So, yeah, it definitely interferes. It really, really does.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself easily distracted by things around you?\n\nPatient: Oh, my goodness, yes. It's actually ridiculous how easily distracted I get. It's almost comical if it wasn't so frustrating. Like, just the other day—and this happens all the time, honestly, it's a daily struggle—but if I’m trying to work at the kitchen table, which is sort of my central command station for all the household bills and those PTA spreadsheets I mentioned earlier... I'll sit down with my laptop, I'll have my coffee, and I'm fully intending to just power through and get it done. \n\nBut then, the tiniest thing happens. My phone will buzz. Just a tiny little vibration against the wood of the table—maybe it's a group text or just an alert about a sale at a craft store—and boom, my attention is just gone. I have to look at it. Or it doesn't even have to be inside the house! A car will drive by outside, maybe it's the delivery truck or just a neighbor driving a little too fast, and I'll look up out the window to see who it is. Next thing I know, I'm staring out at the street, wondering if the mail has come yet or noticing that the bushes need trimming. \n\nAnd sometimes it's not even an external noise, you know? It's my own brain! I'll be right in the middle of typing a sentence, and a totally random thought about dinner will pop into my head. I'll suddenly think, \"Oh, wait, did I take the chicken out of the freezer to thaw?\" or \"Do we have enough of that specific pasta my youngest likes?\" And that one thought can pull me completely off track. I'll get up, walk to the kitchen, start digging through the freezer, maybe reorganize a shelf while I'm in there... and it all happens before I even notice I’ve completely stopped what I was doing. Half an hour will go by, my laptop screen will have gone black, and I'm standing in the kitchen holding a bag of frozen peas, totally derailed from my actual task because every little noise or random thought just completely hijacks my attention.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your restlessness and inability to focus are affecting your relationships with friends and family?\n\nPatient: Well, wait, I mean, I feel like I just went over that a pretty good amount when I was talking about my husband and the PTA ladies, didn't I? I'm not really sure what else you're looking for with that question, to be completely honest. Because, like I was just saying, it's not like I have some secret, estranged family member or a best friend who completely cut me off because of my scattered brain, if that's what you mean. I don't really have any huge, dramatic blow-ups to report. \n\nIt's really just the day-to-day stuff I already poured out to you. It's that constant, exhausting cycle of me over-promising and under-delivering. Like with my husband, it’s just that constant low-level tension I mentioned, where I know he's disappointed that I forgot to do something again, and I feel so incredibly guilty about it. And with my friends, I guess... well, it's just more of the same pattern. I'll be sitting at a coffee shop with a girlfriend, and she'll be pouring her heart out about her kids or something, and my brain is just... gone. I'm bouncing my leg under the table, I'm looking at the barista, I'm thinking about whether I left the hall light on at home. And I know she can tell I'm not fully present, even though I desperately want to be! \n\nBut yeah, I don't really know what else to say about it beyond what I already told you, because it’s all just... it’s all the same thing. Just me feeling like a chaotic burden to the people who care about me, and them having to be overly patient with me. So, I don't know if that answers your question, but beyond what I already went over, I haven't really noticed anything different or new. It just permeates everything in the exact same way.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Give candidates as ICD-10 codes, not disease names.\n- If the list changed from the previous candidates, say in \"note\" what this turn added or ruled out. I try so hard to look composed and just be present in the conversation, but I'm constantly shifting my weight, crossing and uncrossing my legs, adjusting how I'm sitting. I feel like I must look so uncomfortable to everyone else, but really, it's just that staying in one position for more than a few minutes feels almost impossible. Oh, absolutely. It’s actually funny you ask that, because looking back on it now, with everything we've been talking about, it is so incredibly clear that this was already a huge part of me way back in elementary school. Like, I was notoriously *that* girl in class. You know, the one with the absolute disaster of a desk? Whenever the teachers would do desk checks, mine was just a total nightmare. A complete black hole of crumpled-up assignments, broken crayons, loose papers... I could never find a single thing in there when I was asked to take out a specific workbook.

I’d leave them at school, or I’d shove them in my backpack and forget to give them to her, or she’d actually sign it and I’d lose it in that messy desk. I remember I almost missed a field trip to the science museum in fourth grade because she had to rush to the school at the last second to sign a new one in the front office before the bus left. 

But yes, the teachers definitely noticed my behavior, too. They were constantly sending notes home or bringing it up at parent-teacher conferences. It was always the exact same story—they'd say I was a sweet girl, but I just talked out of turn all the time. A thought would pop into my head and I’d just blurt it out without raising my hand, I just couldn't seem to hold it in. And the notes always said I seemed completely unable to stay seated. I was always finding some excuse to get up and wander around the room. I had to sharpen my pencil, or I had to throw a tiny scrap of paper away, or I just *had* to go look at the bulletin board. I just could not keep my body in that chair for the life of me. 

So my parents definitely heard about it, a lot. They mostly just chalked it up to me being a chatty, scatterbrained kid who just had a lot of energy, but yeah, the teachers were definitely flagging it constantly. I actually think my mom still has some of those old report cards in a box somewhere in her attic, and I guarantee if you looked at the 'conduct' section, every single one would say the exact same thing about me needing to stay in my seat and wait my turn to speak...

It was never about me being a bad kid or anything, but they would always write things like, \"She talks out of turn,\" or \"She seems unable to stay seated during lesson time.\" I remember my third-grade teacher—I think her name was Mrs. Davis—she actually had to move my desk right up next to hers because I was constantly up, wandering over to the pencil sharpener even if my pencil was fine, or leaning all the way out of my chair to talk to the kid next to me. \n\nI just couldn't stay glued to the chair. My legs would get that same restless feeling I was just telling you about with the paperwork.
